question: Does the repair compute the checksums encoders write, does a field changed under a checksum get past it afterwards, and does the repair leave alone what it says it leaves alone?
method: `oadec_truehd::Repairer` recomputes, for one access unit, the CRC-16 of the major sync, the check nibble over the header and the directory, the CRC-8 of every restart header the blocks reach, the parity byte and CRC-8 that close a segment, and the check nibble and parity byte of the extra data. To find a restart header's CRC it runs the segment parser with a switch that only this module can set: the parser then records where the CRC is and what it has to be, and reads on. `oadec_eac3::repair::fix_crcs` recomputes crc2 of a syncframe and, in an AC-3 frame, crc1, which sits in front of the five eighths it covers and is found by dividing the register after them by x once for each bit. The hidden `oadec repair` applies them to a stream. Measured: (1) `oadec repair` over the 125 streams of evidence 01, the output compared with the input by SHA-256; (2) the unit and command-line tests; (3) the two fuzz targets that repair their input first, in the seeded run with overflow checks and debug assertions on (RUSTFLAGS="-C debug-assertions=on -C overflow-checks=on", 200,000 rounds a target); (4) the three commands that rewrite an E-AC-3 frame, which now close it with `fix_crcs`, against main on two streams; (5) eight mutations.

a_sound_stream_is_left_as_it_is.the_ten_that_do_not: heads cut inside a frame or a unit; their last 14,612 bytes in all are no whole unit and are copied as they are, and nothing before them needed a checksum written

unit_tests.fixtures: the nine TrueHD and MLP fixtures come out byte for byte, with as many units as the extractor frames
unit_tests.seeded_changes: one to three bits changed in the first forty units of each fixture, 300 times: after a repair no checksum it covers is wrong wherever the units can still be read, and a second repair changes nothing
unit_tests.each_checksum: spoiled alone and put back to the byte it was: major sync CRC, header nibble, segment parity, segment CRC, extra data nibble, extra data parity, and the CRC of a restart header, which is not on a byte
unit_tests.ac3: frames of four sizes built from a header and noise pass both CRC checks of the decoder once fixed; a change in the first five eighths rewrites crc1 and leaves crc2, as the standard intends
unit_tests.left_alone: a bit changed inside an Evolution frame stays changed and the frame's other bytes with it: the one byte written is the parity that closes the wrapping

taken_at_its_word.truehd: one bit of a unit's input timing, and one reserved bit of its directory: `verify` exits 7 with bytes skipped before the repair; after it every unit is framed, nothing is skipped, and the exit code is 0. The timing bit then meets the rule behind the checksum, which reports it as a warning
taken_at_its_word.eac3: one bit in the JOC payload of a frame: before, the first fault is the frame's CRC; after, the CRC holds and the first fault is the JOC payload that no longer parses, which is the fault the change made

fuzz_targets_that_repair_first.seeded_run: seed 0, 200,000 rounds for each of the ten targets, and seeds 1 to 3 for the two that repair first, all with overflow checks and debug assertions on: no failure

libfuzzer.where: the `fuzz` workflow on this pull request, at the commit before this file was completed: Linux, nightly-2026-10-14 (rustc 1.101.0-nightly 822182db4), cargo-fuzz 0.13.2, AddressSanitizer and debug assertions on, the corpus seeded from the fixtures, 90 seconds a target, each target once
libfuzzer.the_pairs: An edge is libFuzzer's unit of coverage, counted over everything linked into the target, the repair's own code included: on the seeds the two targets that repair first stand 168 and 187 edges above their pairs, and that is the repair. From there, in the same 90 seconds, `truehd_unit_repaired` gains 423 edges where `truehd_unit` gains 366, and `truehd_decode_repaired` gains 898 where `truehd_decode` gains 758. One run of each: the direction is what the repair was written for, the size is not a measurement

result.frame_rewriting_commands: `eac3-joc-config`, `eac3-joc-offset` and `eac3-ecpl-inject` on the committed E-AC-3 fixture and on a head of the work directory: the same exit code, the same messages and the same bytes from main and from this branch, six runs of six
result.mutations: eight, all caught: the parser reading on past a restart header whose CRC is wrong (by a test of the parser and one of the repair), the CRC of a restart header written a bit late, the CRC of a major sync computed over the CRC as well, the check nibble computed over the header alone, the segment parity without its constant, the parity byte written into the frame it wraps, crc1 taken back sixteen bits too far, crc2 without the sixteen zero bits

reading: The repair writes what encoders write: on 9.1 million access units and 143 thousand syncframes of real material it has nothing to change, down to the CRC of a restart header that starts two bits into a segment. That is a stronger statement than the tests of the parsers make, which only ever read a checksum; this computes each one from the bytes and lands on the stored value every time. What it buys is reach. A change behind a checksum used to end at the checksum, in the tests and in the fuzzers alike; the two fuzz targets that repair first hand the decoder changed coefficients and samples it would otherwise have replaced by silence. Its limits are stated and tested: the lossless check is left wrong on purpose, because it speaks of the samples, and the keyed protection of the metadata is not computed anywhere in this repository, so a payload changed under it is a payload a real decoder with the key would refuse. A repaired stream is consistent bytes, not restored audio, which is why the command is hidden.
